content.title: About
content.content: Cooked celery consists of stalks that have been peeled and boiled until tender. The cooking process softens the texture while preserving its distinctive aroma, making it easy to digest. It is used in soups, stews, salads, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Celery belongs to the Apiaceae family and is closely related to parsley and dill.
Celery was known in ancient Egypt, where it was used for medicinal purposes.
Celery contains phthalides, compounds responsible for its characteristic scent.
In many cuisines, cooked celery is often served with a cream or sour cream sauce.
Celery can be grown as an annual or a perennial plant.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, helps regulate blood sugar levels, and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low-calorie food
items.content: 100 g of cooked celery provides about 16 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B6, folate, and niacin aid metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of potassium and sodium
items.content: These minerals help maintain fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and vitamin C protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to celery, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Celery can enhance the effects of certain anticoagulants; consult a healthcare professional if you take such medication.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Oxalate content may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible persons.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked celery can be served as a standalone side, added to soups, stews, vegetable casseroles, or diced into salads. It pairs well with lemon juice, olive oil, and soft cheeses.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked celery in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions after cooling.
